newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: Embattled Czech finance minister resigns.
newsitem.headline: Embattled Czech finance minister resigns.

text.p: The Czech Republic's embattled Finance Minister Ivan Kocarnik has bowed to growing pressure for his resignation and quit, Prime Minister Vaclav Klaus said on Saturday.
Kocarnik's resignation came on a day when two other ministers also stepped down during a cabinet shake-up aimed at reviving the government's sagging fortunes in opinion polls.

Klaus told a news conference broadcast live by Czech Radio that 52-year-old Kocarnik, a member of his Civic Democratic Party (ODS), would be replaced by the premier's chief adviser Jiri Waigel, an economist who is not affiliated to any party.

Calls began for Kocarnik to go last year after a rash of financial scandals which resulted in the fall of a number of banks, and intensified earlier this year when the government agreed on a set of spending cuts to avoid a budget deficit.
Nevertheless, Klaus said he did not accept criticism of Kocarnik's record at the ministry.
Klaus also announced the resignation of Interior Minister Jan Ruml, who is to be replaced by Petr Necas, the chairman of the lower house defence and security committee.

A ministerial report this week admitted that the police could not cope with economic crime, over which the opposition has fiercely criticised the government, and that the scale of the problem had been underestimated.
Earlier on Saturday Industry and Trade Minister Vladimir Dlouhy, of junior coalition partner the Civic Democratic Alliance (ODA), also announced his resignation.
Leaders of the three government coalition parties met seperately on Saturday to discuss reshuffling the cabinet, whose support has declined amid worsening economic conditions.

The cabinet reshuffle has been given greater urgency by the battering the Czech crown has received in the foreign exchange markets. On Thursday, it reached a record low six percent below the central bank's mark/dollar parity level.
But the crown rallied strongly on Friday to 0.8 percent below parity, helped by central bank intervention.
Klaus also said the ODS would welcome Michael Zantovsky, elected ODA leader earlier this year after returning from his position as ambassador to Washington, taking a cabinet post.

Zantovsky has been tipped for defence, held by the Christian Democrats, or foreign affairs, held by the ODS. Under the terms of the agreement signed by the three-party ruling coalition, parties can change their own ministers without consulting the others.
"If the ODS could contribute to this by passing one of its portfolios into an exchange (of ministries between coalition parties), I can say the ODS is prepared to do so," Klaus said.

But he added that there had been no talk of Foreign Minister Josef Zieleniec leaving the government during the meeting of the ODS leadership. "Nothing of the kind was discussed during yesterday's or today's talks," he said.
Christian Democrat leader Josef Lux also earlier ruled out making the defence portfolio available.
However, Klaus said he did not rule out that the leaders of the three parties would hold further discussions this weekend.
